I beg to differ. There are so many messages because people who like to
be able to exploit loopholes in the poor cards and rules are upset
because those poor cards and rules are being removed. Anyone who cannot
see that a card can be "broken" would be better served playing Magic.
Jyhad is (or is supposed to be) a balanced game. All barriers to that
balance shall be removed. Two factors should reign supreme when
deciding who wins games: a) Deck construction skill and b) Play skill.
Then, the next factors should be: c) Diplomacy and d) Random chance. A
distant fifth is where I place e) Number of cards owned. Without new
errata, number of cards owned goes up to number 2, behind deck
construction.

-Chris

Yes, it is nice to be completely right all the time.

:-)

Anyway, again, I fail to see how these rulings get in the way of popularizing
the game. New players come into Jyhad by being taught by old players, not by
seeing advertising or reading reviews (as there aren't any...). If, at this
point in time, someone starts playing Jyhad, I would say that 90% of the time,
it is because some old player teaches them how. The people teaching the game
can very easily teach the rulings as well, especially as most of the more
drastic card changes were made to cards that new players will have very little
access to. How many new players are going to have Tombs, RTI, and Mind Rape?
Not many, and I assure you that they will probably be happier that the 3 Tombs
you have are less poweful (due to errata) than the none that they have.

The vast bulk of the errata is fairly simple clarifications and/or minor
changes that are in no way obstructive to learning the game, like Immortal
Grapple, Pulled Fangs, Zip Gun, WWEF, and the vote push rules. The dramatic
and complex rulings A) don't come up all that often and B) mostly affect cards
from currently difficult to aquire expansion cards that new players will have
limited access to (and most of that access will come from older players who can
easily explain the rulings).

Indeed, and i have no problem with the vast bulk of the errata. And i am
in favour of the bits that move the game back to where it was supposed to
be - no direct bleeds except against your predator unless via Night Moves
or Cat Burglary, for example; Rotschreck doing what it actually says it
does; and overturning the absurd idea that you can prevent the Rutor's
Hand damage using combat cards.

But i still disagree with the rewrites. It comes down to a cost-benefit
analysis again.

How likely is it that you are going to be RtI'd next time you play?
How bad is it to be RtI'd?
How likely is it for a new player to be put off by a rules-lawyery oldie?
How bad is it for a new player to be put off by a rules-lawyery oldie?

I can't put numbers on these but it seems to me that the first two are
in-game costs - they only really matter for the particular match that is
currently going on. They have no impact on the game AS A WHOLE. Contrast
with the latter two.

And obviously, i will change my mind if there is a realistic prospect of a
re-issue.

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Legbiter wrote:
"How likely is it that you are going to be RtI'd next time you play?"

In competetive gaming, very likely, and I like to encourage my play group to be
competetive.

"How bad is it to be RtI'd?"

As James pointed out, if RTI is used appropriately (i.e. to maximum abuse
potential), it will oust you when used. That is pretty bad.

"How likely is it for a new player to be put off by a rules-lawyery oldie?"

There is a vast difference between going "Heh heh. Now that you have attempted
to play that RTI to oust me, I will inform you that it does not work the way
you think it does. I beat you! You stupid newbie! Bwahahahah!" and explaining
the rules before you play. It is not at all difficult to explain before
playing a game "the rules have been changed some. Most of the changes are
pretty minor and I'll let you know when they come up, but the following 4 or 5
cards have been changed pretty substantially...". Not difficult at all, and
only off putting to the incredibly impatient and fickle.

"How bad is it for a new player to be put off by a rules-lawyery oldie?"

Again, this does not have anything to do with the rules. If you (not you
specifically) are going to be a jerk, you are going to put off new players.
There are ways to teach new players a game, and all of the good ways involve
letting new players know stuff _before_ you kill them with it.

I only agree with this in part. Jyhad is about playing in a Group Dynamic.
Table talk, bluffing, backstabbing, partnerships..
These are the elements of Jyhad that I take to heart. The cards simply
provide the medium.
This is also why I believe people like myself are opposed to the changing
of (D) Actions by the 7/7 ruling. While it makes for some game consistency
(ie.. Must Kill My Prey!!), it removes some of the crucial FUN from play.
Using the DCI Victory Point system, it generally does me no good to
oust my grand-predator giving someone else that VP that I want for myself.
Yet, in the same instance.. Maybe I need to oust that bugger to put more
pressure on MY predator buying me time.

With the changing of the (D) Action you've made this game an Echo of
Magic:TG. Instead of being a group game, it becomes a two player
game (at a given time). As I recall most folks here agree that Jyhad
is pretty weak as a 2-player game.

The argument about change is simple: Change needs to happen,
Most of us will agree with that simple statement.

Where we disagree is WHEN the game should change, and just
how much. I find it really interesting that people keep spewing
about R. Garfield's intentions for Jyhad vs. V:TES. I met Mr.
Garfield about 2 years ago in Ann Arbor, he had nothing to say
about the V:TES brand and left the impression on me that he
probably created the basic mechanics of the game and then
left a team of others to flesh it out.

I could be wrong in my impression, but even so.. Just because
R. Garfield created the game doesn't mean that his original ideas
were the best (didn't Jyhad get released about the same time as
Legends)? Seems to me Mr. G. still had a lot to learn about the
CCG environ that he had created, and has spent his remaining
focus on whatever game catches his eye at a particular time.

The problem with Change as I see it is simple. Instead of escalation
like in other card games, it will be real easy to fall onto the path of
"De-Escalation". After 6 cards are fixed, 4 months later (like clockwork)
6 more cards will be fixed after they've been deemed to be "UnBalanced".
And so on..

The game cannot be truely fixed until there is a revision (Card text
fixed and actually printed on cards, new rulebook w/o the lame
basic game).

Until all you have left is a game that tastes as good as superglue..
(If you don't believe me, taste some superglue - Though I will not
be held accountable if you choose to do so. ;-)

Bernie Bresnahan

I'm not sure I understand. If you are not a "greedy predator" yourself,
then why do you have those bleed cards in your hand?

Are you saying that the earlier rule limited bleed decks? Seems to me it
enhanced them by giving them extra options.

What you call "direct bleeds" are still possible using a rare card called
"Cat Burglary". "Night Moves" can also be used against your predator.

"Direct Bleeds", as you call them, give far too much reign to spite. I
have seen some hard feelings caused by this sort of tactic. If one is not
doing it to win the game it seems personal. If someone should get ornery,
and decide to do this to me in a game, then I really don't stand a chance,
as it is hard to deal with 2 predators at once.

If you want to beat up on a particular player, then I suggest you use
politics, not bleeds. That way you are more likely to need a consensus of
players, and random spite will be checked.

I once designed a deck where I bled my predator using Misdirection/Legal
Manipulations, and then played Dramatic Upheaval when he was low on pool.
The deck did not win reliably, since it was hard to pull off the dramatic
upheaval at the correct moment, but it sure as hell made sure that my poor
predator lost. He was ALWAYS the first player ousted, even if he was the
best player at the table. My misdirections left him damaged not only
against me, but also against his own predator. Not very fair to him, I
should think. I was in this instance playing to win, not for spite, but
it still does not seem fair.

Votes are re-usable, but each time I block a bleed, it taps me. No player
can survive for long a double assault in the bleed department, and in my
opinion no player should have to. Against such an assault, he will lose
regardless of skill.

Well, since Badger doesn't seem to articulate his points very well, and since
I happen to agree (at least in part) with him on this point, I suppose it's
time for my argument, which I consider to be pretty well thought out. I
think this argument has been made before, and I know that there was a big
fight over (D) bleeds back in the day. Therefore, I'm sure LSJ will not
change his mind on this issue (I've seen LSJ's posts on (D) bleeds).
However, in the interests of completeness, I'll attempt to convince a few
people...

Okay, Jyhad is a game of predator and prey. You bleed your prey, get bled by
your predator. IMO, this aspect was put into the game to get around the
arbitrary "king-making" of multiplayer Magic games. Everyone gangs up on the
weakest player, kills him, repeat until you have a 2-player game. Not much
fun. So, in Jyhad, you are basically fighting one person and defending
yourself from another. This helps remove the randomness, but also waters it
down to a 2-player game, basically. In general, you can simply ignore what
happens to anyone besides your predator or prey. Or can you? You see,
winning the game is not simply a matter of being the last man standing. If
your prey ousts 3 people, then you oust him, you still lose. So, you have to
endeavor to keep the table even until you can sweep it. Political decks can
do it, as damaging votes can target any methuselah. Rush decks can do it, by
destroying all vampires on the table and then slowly ousting everyone in
turn. Bleed decks cannot anymore.

If the person across the table is racking up huge amounts of pool, you must
simply sit and watch. His actions affect you, but you have no way of
affecting him. IMO, this relegates the game more to luck, which is a Bad
Thing. With directed bleeds, you can pop over there and steal from his pool.
This way, the entire table affects you, and you can affect the entire table.
A deck which is gradually becoming unstoppable will win if its predator is
not a fast bleed deck. With directed bleeds, you can say something about
that.

Now, why don't people like directed bleeds. IMO, it is because it makes the
game "too random" and it degenerates into a free-for-all. I think this is
rubbish. As for being too random, I believe it is completely the opposite,
for the above reasons. A skillful player need no longer lose just because
his predator is inept and his grand-predator is racking up pool like you
wouldn't believe. A player can no longer ignore half of the table when
playing, but must take into account everything on the board. Forcing more
thought is also, IMO, a Good Thing.

As for the game becoming a free-for-all, I can't see why. You only gain VP's
and pool for ousting your prey. This is plenty of incentive to bleed your
prey. What reason is there to force it? Bleeding your predator or
grand-predator does only one thing: slow them down. If you are stupid enough
to oust them, then you have done no good, and have actually hurt yourself. A
good player will not do this unless it is absolutely necessary. As long as
I've played, I have only rarely seen a bleed directed at a non-prey. It's
simply not a good thing to do most times. But when it *is* useful, I don't
see why a methuselah should be denied the option.

Am I missing anything here?

One problem I see a lot is not picking a few pool from someone who's
getting ahead, but no-holds-barred ganging up on someone for no reason.
I see it in board games, and I see it in Jyhad with cross-table
bleeding. "AAH! He's got a Rush deck! Somebody go bleed him for 20!"
Non-bounce bleed defense is hard enough without having to worry about
defending against _everyone_ at the table. I think cross-table bleeding
makes bleeding too versatile.

> But the point is, you can.

No, I think the point is, the effect is usually much less useful than a
bleed. For a combat deck to really _hurt_ someone, you have to put
_all_ of their vampires into torpor, otherwise they'll just be rescued.
If you bleed someone, you have directly affected their pool.

> This is my biggest argument in favour of cross-table bleeds. If cross-table

> fuss? Why should you take away a weapon that is not all that powerful? Is
> there really a need to remove a player's strategic decisions when usually the
> decision that is currently enforced is the best one?

Because cross-table bleeds are harder to defend against than prey
bleeds. The proactive defenses (rush the bleeders, incapacitate the
bleeders, etc.) are completely useless, since you won't be able to see
the bleed coming.

> > And the cross-table bleed required the least effort, and was hence
> > arguably the most successful way to attack cross-table.
>
> Not true at all. A cross-table bleed still requires just as much effort as a
> prey-bleed, with much less payoff. In fact, it's nearly impossible to get any
> benefit from a cross-table bleed without giving someone else an even greater
> benefit.

It is often worth giving someone else a victory point to get an annoying
deck off the table. The deck with 4 Anarch Revolts that will kill you
next turn, for example. You'll gladly oust it yourself, just to keep
yourself alive.

> he keeps bleed bouncing you, would you bleed with a whole bunch of weenies to
> slow him down?" Sometimes you need to take matters into your own hands.

But I don't think "taking matters into your own hands" is a good thing
at all. This is the only way to directly affect someone else's pool.
Voting involves the whole table, and rushing doesn't affect pool.
Basically the cross-table bleed makes the bleed deck more versatile (and
hence more powerful), and I think this is _too_ much versatility.

I think that's because all of the arguments occured years ago when the

> All I've seen is some doomsday predicitions about cross-table chaos.

> rulings. In fact, I rarely ever see cross-table bleeds at all.

The cross-table bleed usually has a "king-maker" kind of effect. The

tips the balance of the rest of the table.

> about to be ousted, it is up to everyone who is not his predator to save him
> (barring extreme circumstances, such as when leaving that person in the game
> is more detrimental than allowing his predator to gain a VP and 6 pool).

Huh!? Why should you care if someone across the table is being ousted?
You can't always get every single victory point, you know.

> >
> > 1. Without the pressure on your back, you easily oust a few people.
> > B. The inept predator is easily ousted, and then you can deal with the

bleed deck, and the other two decks at the table were also rush combat
decks. I knew that if I was allowed to go one-on-one with my prey, I
would be able to kill him. So I allowed my predator to be ousted by his
predator, and then I allowed that person to be ousted himself. I got
the remaining two victory points. It seems to me like you're trying to
sweep every table you sit down at...

> > No, it usually either makes them angry or kills them.

> You can't make allowances for stupidity. The only

Please forgive the long post,

Since the games inception my play group has allowed directed actions (bleeds,
whatever) to occur across the table. This has never caused a problem but has instead
added a great a amount of versatility to the game. Most of the (D) bleed based
actions that occur in our group serve the purpose of weakening a competitor not
killing them (ie. a political deck that is really starting a large build and
accumulating a large pool, a combat deck bringing out his 5th large vampire and
smashing his prey). At one point you must deal with this political monster or
gangrel with 6 vampires and 3 garou. Having this capability doesn't impact the small
game, because there is simply no application to it. In a large game this changes the
dynamic drastically. Many deals come about because of (D) actions (ie. If I bleed
and weaken your predator will you vote for me?, I bleed someone who is totally
disconnected from me just to get the edge, I weaken another political deck so that
I may acheive political dominance, on and on).

" The deck with 4 Anarch Revolts that will kill you next turn, for example. You'll

gladly oust it yourself, just to keep yourself alive." 100% correct if that vampire
is affecting my pool I will snuff them as soon as possible. This breeds a need for a
more complex strategy. If you know that everyone at the table will object to your
playing 4 anarch revolts then you will think before you do and attempt to time the
anarchs revilts with other actions to acheive the same obejctive.

The use of this strategy makes common sense. I am a very powerful vampire
controlling other weaker vampires. Who is to say that if I the capability to do so
(ie. a card) that I couldn't bleed any other vampire that I choose.

"For a combat deck to really _hurt_ someone, you have to put _all_ of their

vampires into torpor, otherwise they'll just be rescued." 6 rescued vampires with no
blood does a deck little good. Their deck has been crippled

"Cross-table bleeds are harder to defend against than prey bleeds. The proactive

defenses (rush the bleeders, incapacitate the bleeders, etc.) are completely

useless, since you won't be able to see the bleed coming." Again you are correct (D)
bleeds are much more diffucult to defend against however that does not nessecitate
their exclusion. I can tap a vampire and intercept a (D) action whats the problem.
(D) actions 99% will not occur consistently. Why continually bleed the guy across
the table from you. Once in a while for strategic advantage it makes perfect sense
consistently bashing the guy across the table from you gets doesn't kill your prey.

"Basically the cross-table bleed makes the bleed deck more versatile." Again 99% of
the time heavy bleed decks don't want to waste their time across the table when they
could spend those bleed cards on squashing their prey. They want the pool. They want
a quick kill. BTW a heavy bleed deck smashing their prey is the perfect target for a
cross table bleed. It slows down their strategy and forces them to either defend
themselves or bleed you in retaliation. Either way, less pressure on their prey.

"Why should you care if someone across the table is being ousted?" I dont care
about the VP. I care about that another player is getting pool and thereby
strengthening themselves against my eventual attack. General rule: I want all the
blood points and if I can't have them then no one else should either.

There has been an occasion when I have snuffed my predator. It depends upon what
your predator is doing. If he has a combat deck and you have a voting deck (and are
almost out of S:CE) then killing him in favor of your new predator being another
politcal deck sometimes it is very strategically sound. You simply have to be
careful to not create a predator that you can't control.

Chris

Messages.Author: Alan Flesch
Messages.Body:
I am against cross-table bleeds. I have used them on
occasion, trying it to find some 'advantage' to doing
so, and haven't found too many.

Many multi-player games display what I call the
'Akira Kurosawa' problem. That is, there is a long,
slow, and patient development of resources, and then
one huge, climactic, overwhelming battle; the game
is then won by the person who committed least to the
battle and conserved most of his forces.

Jyhad seeks to side-step this problem in a two-fold
system : the predator/prey mechanic and what I call
the primary/secondary resource split.

The predator/prey mechanic has been discussed elsewhere
as the primary tactic by which the Kurosawa problem
is averted. Every person in play has a target, and every
person in play has a predator. Outside of this pyramid
are effects which have an effect on your position, but
for the most part, they are secondary concerns (to be
viewed in the long-run as future predators/prey). There
are exceptions to this, of course : Antidiluvian Awakening,
Anarch Revolt, and Smiling Jack are the primary
examples. The Anarch Revolt deck is effective because
of its circumvention of the predator/prey mechanic, but
the deck is difficult to win consistently with due to its
non-directability.

The primary/secondary resource split is a bit more complex
to explain. Jyhad has one primary resource : pool. With
pool, secondary resources are purchased (Vamps, equipment,
allies, etc). These secondary resoures often can contribute
back to your pool (Hunting Ground/Blood Doll being the
primary example). Minions (a secondary resource) are used to
attack the primary resource of your prey and secondary resources
of anyone else. Occasionally, they may attack primary resources
(ie. vote decks) but these non-prey primary resource attacks
are more difficult to perform (a vote require a successful
action, and then a successful vote. Often the deck attempts
to minimize the second requirment with cards such as Awe or
by having many titled vampires, but the the condition of
a successful vote still requires a two successes for the effect to
occur).

A combat deck attempts to win by eliminating the secondary
resources of the predator/prey. It attempts to weaken his
own predator to the benefit of his grand-predator; it attempts
to weaken its prey by eliminating defenses to its non-stealth
bleeds. The strength of a combat-deck is all on the secondary-
resource level. Hence, assaults on the secondary resources outside
of the predator/prey pyramid have a small impact on the game
environment. No rush deck is going to systematically take out
every vampire in play, nor is it going to concentrate on eliminating
the vampires of those who aren't harming it. Tactical advantages
of eliminating vampires outside of the predator/prey pyramid
weaken the other Methuselah without bringing its primary
resource reserve into jeopardy. Granted that the Meth in question
may expend its primary resources to recover its secondary, but
this relies on the judgement of the target Methuselah himself,
not the acting Methuselah (ie. the rush-combat player).
Not only that, but vampires are resilient; a combat deck,
unless it places all of a rivals vampires in torpor, will soon
be faced with these vampires returning to play as they
are rescued and slowly rebuild strength. An out-of-pyramid
rush attack will place an offending vampire in torpor
(most times) but with time the minion may be recovered later.

A bleed deck, however, attempts to win by eliminating the
primary resource reserve of his prey while holding off his
predator with other measures ( bleed bounce usually). It weakens
its target on both the primary and secondary resource level. By
reducing the primary resource reserve, it not only brings the
target closer to elimination but closes off the opportunities to
bring new resources into play. Its attacks, when successful,
are more efficient than the rush-deck player (especially since
blood can be regained by vampires weakened by combat via
the hunting action, but pool requires a more sophisticated action
sequence to replenish). A bleed is more difficult to recover
from, especially if the bleed is large enough to place the
recipient in jeopardy of ousting by a single successful bleed.
It has directly brought the recipient of a cross-table bleed closer
to defeat in a way that is not reproducable by the rush-deck
player. (A rush deck usually has little reason to burn
vampires out of the predator/prey pyramid unless his
prey is on the verge of defeat and the rush-deck player has
already begun working on his grandprey).

In short, the benefit gained from an out-of-pyramid bleed is
excessive to the benefit gained from an out-of-pyramid rush.
The rush can only effect secondary-resources which usually leaves
the recipient of the action some recovery options. It slows down
the deck without giving the target's predator too gross an
advantage. The bleed directly effects the primary resource
pool, and can place the predator of the target an enormous
game advantage.

Alan (aj)

>>A deck should not have to defend against everyone at the table.

No, it shouldn't. A deck should have to work out who it's most likely
competitors will be (ie which people on the table will be ousted by
someone else before this deck has to deal with them) and keep only the
cards it needs to defend itself from the others. Otherwise, you'll end
up wasting pool/action on combat cards (Flak Jacket, say) simply because
there is a combat deck on the table, even if there is very little chance
of you and it ever coming in direct competition. And these
pool/actions/master phase actions/whatever will work to the detriment of
the bleed defence I have, being as I won't be able to play it because
I've wasted my time defending myself from everyone on the table.

The point of the predator-prey dynamic as Richard Garfield created it
was to prevent a cross-table free for all. You are supposed to oust
your prey, not someone else's. Only exceptional decks/circumstances
would demand something else (eg ousting someone's prey so you can claim
that victory point back off them with your life (I think) boon you
played earlier).

A deck has to focus on its strategy, and on defending itself from its
likely predators/preys. It shouldn't be defending itself from everyone.

>>OK. I'll say it again. Unless you (a) go jumping across the table
>yourself or (b) have reactive bleed defense, you CANNOT >defend against a
>cross-table bleed.
>
>OK I'll say it again. So what. Your lack of defense is not the issue. The
>fact that it CAN be defended against is the issue.

The point is, you then have the equivalent of TWO predators. If your
deck is so well stocked with bleed defence as to be able to cope with
two predators, I'd like to be able to see you do anything else. And you
might not even be able to predict, early on in the game, who that second
predator will be so you can put any defence down against him.

BTW, if I created a card that said "(D) Oust a Methuselah who is not
you, your predator or prey. This action may only be blocked by
Samantha" and it ousts you, your lack of defence is not the issue. The
fact that it CAN be defended against is the issue. Nope, actually, you
should be defending against STRATEGIES not CARDS. I should be defending
against people doing damage to my minions, not against people using
Thrown Sewer Lid, Torment the Soul, Body of Sun, Sub Machine Gun,
Weather Control, Wolf Companion, Meat Cleaver and Sacrament of Carnage
all individually. I should be thinking - how do I deal with damage?
From strikes? From environmental sources? Maybe damage dealt outside of
combat? How will I get blood back from that?

With bleed I should be thinking - How will I deal with bleeds? Reduce
it? Block it? Torporise them? Banish them? Shift myself to another
position on the table? Burn the large bleeders with Justicar
Retribution? I shouldn't be thinking "How do I deal with Govern the
Unaligned? How do I deal with Bonding? How do I deal with Legal
Manipulations? How do I deal with Pulse of the Canaille?" I should be
thinking of strategies.

Jyhad has *never* been about dealing with specific cards, until the
introduction of the broken cards. Before then, all counters were
counters to strategies, not cards. It was very rare to see r.g.t-c.j
arguing about how to deal with specific cards, unless they were given as
an *example* of a strategy.

I don't think this is the best way to describe it. As the ideal
strategic player, you want everyone to be just weak enough that they
are about to die when they become your prey. (ie, you want everyone
to stay alive until you oust your initial prey; then you want your
new prey to be as weak as possible, etc.)

Simply weakening everyone at the table while gaining power yourself may
not win you the game. If other people get too weak, someone else might
pick up too many victory points for you to win.

In most cases, it is counterproductive for you to oust (or even bring
closer to ousting) anyone other than your prey, because that gives
someone else a victory point and six pool to better compete with you
for the win.

The times that it's most useful to oust someone not your prey is if
they look like turning out to be the winner of the table - that is,
they seem to be the best player with the best deck. In this case,
it may be advantageous to everyone else at the table to gang up on
them until they're dead.

But that's not very fun for the good player, is it?

We 'anti-CTB' people feel that less potential for playing kingmaker is
better, to some extent. The best player at the table *should* win
the game; it should not be easy for the rest of the table to prevent
them from winning by working together. Games that allow full interaction
between all players tend to be determined solely by diplomatic ability,
believable lying, things like that. If you feel (as we do) that
in-game skill is what *should* be most emphasized, then limits on
interaction are a good thing.

That's why the predator-prey dynamic exists in the first place - to
encourage people to concentrate on a particular subset of the people
in the game. It is also why CTB should not be allowed: It allows
too much interaction, at too influential a level, to be good for
the game.

Voting and Bum's Rushes *can* be used across the table. But with
combat, the level of impact is clearly lower than the impact a
cross-table bleed typically has on the recipient. With voting,
the impact can be as great; the only justification I can offer here
is the full-table nature of the voting process - that is, voting
inherently is a full-interaction aspect of the game, since every
player can vote in every vote (at least in theory).

I believe that there's a very good article about this in Duelist by said
Mr Garfield in one of his back page slots. Fairly old issue, I believe.
I'll drag it out next time I get a chance when I'm at home. I think it
uses the example of War or some such game, with the results above.
Whoever was perceived as the biggest threat was ganged up on. Is it
mentioned in Darkness Unveiled too? The game degenerates into "I'm not
the threat, he's the threat!"

But in the same article he does a wonderful thing with counters. Take
three players. Give each one a counter. Choose a player to start.
When it is their turn, they choose another player. That player loses a
counter from his pool. A player with no counters in their pool loses.
Play then proceeds clockwise.

If you give each player 1 counter, the first person to play CANNOT win
the game but they get to choose both who wins and who doesn't win. The
position of kingmaker.

Now, if you give all three players, say, thirty counters, it's basically
down to whichever one is ganged up on. If player A and player B decide
to gang up on player C, then it only takes 15 turns for him to be ousted
because A and B both get rid of him on their turns. Player C, though,
is still in a very powerful position. He has 14 turns at his disposal
(he is ousted by player B's 15th turn so doesn't get his 15th turn
himself). What does he do with his 14 turns? 7 each? All on B? All
on A? In any case, he chooses who wins. Kingmaker again.

Now, think about this in terms of Jyhad. Player A should be getting rid
of Player B. Player B, C. Player C, A. It gives less of an incentive
for two players to gang up on another player (which creates its own,
real life problems if you're not careful). If a player received 6 extra
counters each time he got rid of his prey, he has a definite incentive
to do so.

Of course, in Jyhad, things aren't so simple. It isn't a case of
choosing a player and they lose a pool. You can lose more pool. You
can reduce the amount of pool. You can make it easier to get said
reductions through (combat, stealth, unblockability). You can make it
harder for someone to bleed you (Telepathic Counter, permanent/transient
intercept). But if you have cross table bleeding at the drop of a hat
then it becomes the counter game. Superior play, cardsmanship, deck
crafting, metagame judging, when to contest or yield, when to discard
and so forth be damned. We'll all just gang up on someone with such
skills. And then, what incentive would there be for them to play?
Having to play more badly so that people don't oust them first (say,
after 45 minutes)? Having to hide their very good deck just for the
sake of prolonging the game?

I'd like to know how people who support ct-bleeds feel about this
situation.

In a group I played in for about a year, my combat decks were perhaps
the most feared. This could be partly due to my bluffing ability.
One player that was especially prone be being bluffed was a person
we called the Minion. If the Minion were my grand prey, by merely leaning
over, looking at his vampires, and then saying, "Andy, I think you should
bleed my prey for me." And he would do it. And that person would be
gone and out of the game.

Usually, the ousted person would be very frustrated both at the Minion and
in general. The main reason they had been ousted was because they were
seated between the Minion and myself because of a die roll. Often, the
Minion could be gotten to do things that were equivalent to losing the game
on purpose and served no benefit to him whatsoever.

Now, let's say you are at a tournament. In one round, you are seated with
a bleeding deck as your prey and a viscious combat deck as your predator.
Now your predator, rushes a nice vampire of yours and destroys it. He then
leans over to your prey and says, "If you don't bleed my prey, I'll do the
same to your vampires, too. If you do this, I'll let you oust your prey/my
predator, so you can have a victory point." Now, true, many people will
probably just say "Screw you." However, some people are going to be the
Minion, and you're now facing two predators. More often than not (probably
95%), you are going to be ousted. Does this seem exactly right to you?
After all, against a single well built combat deck, you will at least have
a chance if you built in some combat defense. But against two players, forget
it.

So what does the elimination of cross-table bleeding accomplish? First,
it prevents bleeding for spite. Maybe that player across the table put
a point of that KRC on you last turn, and you didn't like it. Now, tough,
you've got to oust your prey before you can get to him. Second, it eliminates
possible collusion between friends who end up at the same table. Third, it
eliminates intimidation by a dominant deck on a person that may not be as
strong willed.

Sure, this last aspect isn't entirely eliminated, but it confines it only to
certain circumstances: Combat Prey/Bleeding Predator, Combat Prey or
Predator/Voting Predator or Prey. And considering that one of the best
voting clans has the best combat defense (Ventrue with Presence and
Fortitude), the last possibility isn't that great with a well constructed
deck.

Mike

In a *purely* political game, the winner is *always* determined by
who plays politics most effectively. In a game with freer interaction,
the game is more frequently determined by political aspects than in
a game with more limited interaction.

That's why limiting interaction can be a good thing. It focuses
attention more on the non-political aspects of the game. (Therefore
many people think it's possible to have 'too much' interaction, though
they certainly might disagree about how much is too much.)

Having some interaction (in particular, at the level of table talk,
trash talk, threats, and promises) is one of the purposes of playing
games with more than two players, yes. But the maximum possible amount
of interaction is probably not the most desirable amount. (Check
out the article featuring Richard Garfield's illustrative game
with counters to see why not.)

Don't forget that it is not simply (D) Bleed that has become limited, but
rather that (D) doesn't mean that it can be directed at anybody, i.e. the
omnidirectability of (D) as been removed, which is *the original intent of
the rule* (which, in the mind of most, is a good thing). You need specific
card text to overide this (like "(D) Attack any minion").

It doesn't require any rewritting of cards (except those that were written
with this the superflous omnidirectability rule in mind). However,
changing Deflection, TM or other bleed bounce cards require errata, and
people prefer to avoid that except when play balance is compromised.

But, to be able to use bleed bounce to "bleed somebody else", you first
need someone who bleeds you, which is not that easy to have as a bleed card
with the omnidirectability rule. So those cards are still balanced.

But can you? If my deck is working on the principle that I have one
predator at once, I might put bleed defence in so that I can stop a
couple of a bleeds a turn - intercept, bounce, reduction, reduce stealth
etc. So, assuming a reasonably good shuffle, I get a couple of cards a
turn (not necessarily in hand, because of playing cards, drawing new
ones) coming my way. Okay, so let an arbitrary number of cards, X,
represent the number of cards I've allocated to stopping bleeds. Now,
if someone gets the hump at me for doing something nasty, they decide to
start bleeding me - or, as noted elsewhere in this thread, you get The
Minion bleeding you. However, it happens, you end up with two people
bleeding you.

Now, my X cards of bleed defence were working around one predator. I
draw enough cards every turn to put up a fight against ONE predator. To
draw enough to stop two predators, I'd have to put 2X in, more or less.

So, I've got 90 cards in my deck. 90-X cards are cards not allocated to
bleed defence. If I have to go to 90-2X cards for the rest of my deck,
it gets harder to play it. I have to start making a deck with more and
more bleed defence in it simply because I'm a good player (I'm not - I
can theorise but my actual playing skills let me down a fair bit). So,
a player who gets ganged up on has to start not playing the game and
start acting defensively. So, my deck which was good fun to play now
gets people ganging up on me. I have to put more defence in, making my
deck less likely to do what it wants, or just die, making the game less
fun for me. Cross-table votes are harder to pull off now, because of
the No Vote Pushing rules (see another post of mine in this thread about
the social interaction of votes). And combat is still very difficult to
pull off effectively and though it puts me in a more vulnerable
position, a cross table rush doesn't bring my pool closer to an ousting
level.

>enviroment I may very well choose to protect one of my fellow methuselahs.
>This also adds depth to the game.
>

help another Methuselah, but it works to the detriment of another
Methuselah. I fail to see how a cross-table bleed actually "protects"
them though. The vampires preying on it are just as liable to do damage
to it, they just might leave one or two more untapped to block. On the
other hand, their predator might just think "Blow it - if people are
ganging up on me cross-table then I'm going to be ousted. I might as
well just take him out now and to hell with the consequences. I came to
play my deck and I'm not going to stop playing it just because other
people on the table can't actually play the game and so have to gang up
on me."

First of all, it is hardly the case that cross-table bleeding is the
only possible diplomatic tactic. But directly depleting someone's pool
from across the table when they can't reliably defend against it is
simply too useful. Cross-table voting and attacking are fine for the
same reasons that you feel ct-bleeds are fine. But votes can be voted
down, especially when they go across the table, and a combat can at
worst burn a vampire. But bleeding directly affects someone's pool, and
unless that person is playing with Deflections or intercept, they're
having undue pressure put on them. And it's not fair to say "that's
person's doing well" or "I don't like that person" and have the result
be a ct-bleed.

Cross-table bleeds were never intended to be a part of this game. They
bring too much interaction into play, and prevent people with skill from
being able to do well. If you sit down at a table and somehow everyone
else is convinced that you must die, there won't be anything you can do
about it; they'll cross-table bleed you to death out of their own
paranoia.

In your own group, you know better than anyone else the personality and
temprament of the players. But in a tournament setting the rules should
(a) reflect original intent and (2) provide a balanced fair environment.

James

We're not adocating rules changes because they make certain decks better
or worse. They improve the quality of the game by making it more
balanced. By "balanced" I don't mean balanced between good players and
bad, or between good decks and bad; I mean balanced in the sense that no
strategy has a distinct advantage over another. Then good game play and
clever, effective decks win tournaments; not broken cards and broken
rules.

> clear that V:TES' designers never intended to allow ct bleeds.

Right. An equivalent limitation are the rules on who can block certain
actions. Normally only your predator and your prey can block you, unless
an action is directed, in which case only the target can block.

In the case of Blocking, special cards like Eagle's Sight were created to
allow circumvention of these rules. One needed superior Auspex to use the
ability, indicating that designers took the restrictions seriously, and
thought that they should not be easy to break.

In the case of Bleeding, the special cards Cat Burglary and Night Moves
were printed to get around the rules specifying who could be bled. Both
cards limit the bleed to 1, again indicating that the designers clearly
felt that ct bleeds required serious limitation.
